summary: CHICK TO MARS is a mobile-first, interactive space exploration and colony-building game in which players help a fictional chick survive on the Moon and eventually establish a habitat on Mars. The experience combines resource management, science-based challenges, mini-games, and educational modules grounded in selected NASA mission archives and publicly available datasets. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data, Mars mission instruments, AI4MARS terrain classifications, Artemis II lunar observations, and NASA human-system risk research inform the game's missions and learning content. The project aims to make space science and scientific data approachable for young learners while clearly distinguishing verified mission facts from fictional gameplay simulations.
details:
1. PROJECT STORY — IT ALL STARTED WITH A CHICK!

Imagine an ordinary office employee working at NASA.

Every morning, the employee arrives at work, performs routine duties in mission control, and sits at a computer. However, there is one enormous problem that seems impossible to solve: a pet chick!

This tiny chick turns its owner's working life into a nightmare. It wanders across desks, jumps onto keyboards, interferes with computers, and constantly causes unexpected problems.

At first, these incidents seem minor, but they gradually escalate. Tasks are interrupted, missions become confused, and the employee's performance deteriorates. Eventually, the employee is fired from NASA.

Now comes the final day at work...

As the employee leaves NASA after years of service, all that frustration is directed at the little chick.

The employee thinks:

“If you've caused me this much trouble, let's see how you manage in space!”

And so the revenge plan begins: the employee sends the chick to the Moon aboard one of NASA's rockets!

This event is an entirely fictional and humorous introduction to the game. It does not depict actual NASA employees or a real NASA mission.

The rocket reaches the Moon. The chick is now alone, far away from Earth, in an unfamiliar environment.

But the story does not end there.

The chick refuses to give up. It explores the lunar surface, uses the resources available, learns to produce water and food, manages power and oxygen systems, develops new technologies, and discovers science-based solutions to survive.

Over time, its goal changes:

Survival is no longer enough. The chick now wants to reach Mars and build a new habitat there!

The player guides the chick through this journey. In an adventure spanning the Moon and Mars, the player explores, manages resources, completes missions, and learns from real space research.

A humorous story of revenge thus becomes a space-exploration adventure grounded in authentic scientific knowledge.

 

2. HIGH-LEVEL PROJECT OVERVIEW

CHICK TO MARS is a mobile-first space exploration and colony-development game designed to teach players about lunar and Martian exploration in an entertaining, accessible, and interactive way.

Players guide a small chick that has been sent to the Moon through its struggle to survive and reach Mars. To succeed, they generate resources, upgrade a base, conduct scientific investigations, explore different planetary environments, and complete missions.

A defining feature of the project is its integration of historical and recent NASA scientific information, mission records, and space research into the gameplay experience.

Selected information from NASA's open-data resources is presented through NASA Data Lab, Space Archive, exploration missions, rover activities, and environmental simulations.

Rather than simply reading about space, players attempt to solve in-game problems inspired by genuine scientific discoveries.

The main purpose of CHICK TO MARS is to spark young people's interest in space science and encourage them to explore scientific data through play.

3. THE PROBLEM AND WHY THE PROJECT MATTERS

NASA generates vast amounts of scientific data during space exploration. These records encompass lunar surface maps, the Martian atmosphere, rover imagery, temperature measurements, astronaut observations, and many other topics.

However, because much of this material is published in technical formats and specialized scientific terminology, younger users may find it difficult to explore independently.

CHICK TO MARS addresses this challenge through a gamified educational approach.

One of the project's most important features is the integration of historical and recent NASA scientific data into the gaming experience.

The project does not merely describe historic NASA missions; it brings selected scientific data products, observations, maps, and recent mission archives into its educational and exploratory features.

For example:

·   Lunar landforms are linked to data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO).

·   Martian elevation and terrain information is explored using MOLA data from the Mars Global Surveyor mission.

·   Martian surface terrain categories are connected to the AI4MARS dataset.

·   Lunar observations from Artemis II are introduced as recent scientific content in the game's Space Archive.

·   Astronaut health and living conditions are explained in the Warning Guide using NASA's Human System Risks research.

Through this approach, NASA data is not confined to a bibliography; it becomes part of the player's process of discovery.

The project aims to turn scientific knowledge from passive reading into active investigation, decision-making, and problem-solving.

4. INTEGRATION OF NASA DATA INTO THE GAME

CHICK TO MARS connects selected resources from NASA's open-data archives and mission records with different gameplay systems.

The goal is not to download every NASA archive into the game, but to select scientifically meaningful data products, attribute them accurately, and translate them into understandable interactions.

4.1. Lunar Data — Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) mission has been studying the lunar surface since 2009 [7].

The game draws in particular on information from the following scientific instruments:

LOLA — Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter

LOLA measures lunar surface elevations, slopes, and topographic characteristics. These measurements provide a scientific foundation for the game's lunar maps and surface-exploration missions.

LROC — Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera

LROC provides high-resolution imagery of the lunar surface. The imagery informs educational content about craters, surface structures, and potential landing sites.

Diviner Lunar Radiometer

Diviner investigates the thermal characteristics of the lunar surface. Its observations support educational explanations of temperature and environmental conditions in the game.

LEND — Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector

LEND contributes to research on the distribution of hydrogen and possible water-ice resources on the Moon.

Together, these datasets help players understand landforms, temperatures, and potential resource-rich regions while exploring the Moon.

NASA's September 2026 LRO Data Release 67 includes data products from LOLA, LROC, Diviner, LEND, and other instruments [3].

4.2. Mars Data

The Mars exploration features draw on several NASA missions and instruments [8].

MOLA — Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter

MOLA measured elevations across the Martian surface. Its measurements are used to understand Martian maps, valleys, craters, and terrain formations.

TES — Thermal Emission Spectrometer

TES studied thermal-infrared radiation emitted from the Martian surface and atmosphere. Its observations support research into mineral composition, temperature, and atmospheric properties.

REMS — Rover Environmental Monitoring Station

REMS is an environmental monitoring instrument suite aboard the Curiosity rover. It provides information on Martian weather and environmental changes.

ChemCam

ChemCam is a scientific analysis instrument aboard the Curiosity rover. It helps investigate the chemical composition of Martian rocks and soil.

MAVEN IUVS — Imaging Ultraviolet Spectrograph

The IUVS instrument aboard MAVEN studies the upper layers of the Martian atmosphere and processes associated with atmospheric escape.

These sources form a scientific basis for the game's discussions of the Martian atmosphere, terrain surveys, rock analysis, and environmental exploration.

4.3. AI4MARS — Intelligent Terrain Recognition

AI4MARS is a NASA-published dataset containing images captured by Mars rovers.

It comprises approximately 35,000 images and 326,000 semantic-segmentation image labels [9, 23].

The dataset was developed to classify terrain types in imagery collected by the Curiosity, Opportunity, and Spirit rovers.

Its approach serves as a reference for Rover Rescue and other terrain-exploration missions in the game.

Players learn to recognize different types of terrain and consider how a rover should navigate varying surface conditions.

4.4. Artemis II — Recent Lunar Exploration

Artemis II is one of the project's most significant recent sources of mission data.

NASA's Artemis II mission launched on April 1, 2026, and ended when the crew returned to Earth on April 10, 2026 [5].

Four astronauts traveled around the Moon, observed its far side, and collected numerous scientific images and records.

On October 7, 2026, NASA released more than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data to researchers and the public [1, 2].

The archive contains more than 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, approximately 8.5 hours of audio recordings of scientific observations, and images annotated by the crew [1, 6].

CHICK TO MARS connects selected materials from these observations to the Space Archive and lunar-exploration missions.

In an Artemis II-inspired special mission, players experience an educational version of the Orion spacecraft's journey around the Moon.

The Moon's far side, craters, variations in surface features, and observation activities are presented in gamified form.

An important scientific distinction must be maintained: Artemis II was a crewed lunar flyby, not a mission that entered a complete, sustained orbit around the Moon. The game's 360-degree exploration path is a simplified simulation created for educational purposes.

5. TEN SIGNIFICANT SPACE MISSIONS AND DEVELOPMENTS

CHICK TO MARS presents ten important missions and developments in its in-game Space Archive to teach the history of space exploration in chronological and interactive form.

These missions are not presented merely as information cards. Each is connected to mini-missions, discovery activities, scientific explanations, and player progression.

1. Opportunity Rover — 2018–2019

NASA's Opportunity rover lost contact with Earth during a massive dust storm affecting Mars in June 2018.

NASA announced the end of the mission on February 13, 2019 [10].

In the game, the player acts as a researcher investigating Opportunity's final mission records, exploring the effects of dust storms on rovers and the importance of solar-power systems.

The game's rescue scenario is fictional. In reality, Opportunity was not recovered.

2. InSight — 2018–2022

NASA's InSight lander touched down on Mars in 2018 to investigate the planet's interior [11].

Its seismic measurements were used to study marsquakes and the internal structure of Mars.

Players take part in a scientific-analysis mission that challenges them to interpret Martian seismic information.

3. Perseverance Rover — 2021

Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater on February 18, 2021 [12].

Among its primary objectives are searching for signs of past microbial life and collecting rock and regolith samples that could potentially be returned to Earth in the future.

Players explore Jezero Crater, identify scientifically interesting rocks, and participate in sample-collection missions.

4. Ingenuity Mars Helicopter — 2021–2024

On April 19, 2021, Ingenuity completed the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.

Although originally designed as a five-flight technology demonstration, it completed 72 flights. Its mission ended in January 2024 [13].

In the game, players conduct aerial reconnaissance above Mars to identify suitable routes for a rover.

5. DART — 2022

On September 26, 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos, demonstrating that a kinetic impact can alter the motion of a celestial body.

Players complete an educational mission about planetary defense and asteroid motion [14].

6. Artemis I — 2022

Artemis I was the first integrated flight test of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and Orion spacecraft.

It launched on November 16, 2022, and concluded on December 11, 2022 [15].

Players learn the fundamentals of rocket systems, spacecraft mission planning, and the stages of a flight around the Moon.

7. OSIRIS-REx — 2023

OSIRIS-REx delivered a sample collected from asteroid Bennu to Earth on September 24, 2023 [16].

The mission demonstrates the scientific value of asteroid sample return and the study of the early Solar System.

Players take part in sample-collection and scientific-analysis activities.

8. Europa Clipper — 2024

Europa Clipper launched on October 14, 2024 [17].

The mission aims to investigate Jupiter's icy moon Europa and determine whether it has conditions that could support life.

The game includes a scientific exploration activity about Europa's icy surface and ocean worlds.

9. Blue Ghost Mission 1 — 2025

Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost Mission 1 successfully landed on the Moon on March 2, 2025 [18].

Under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative, the mission carried scientific and technological instruments to the lunar surface.

Players learn about the purposes of scientific instruments deployed on the Moon and the systems involved in lunar exploration.

10. Artemis II — 2026

Artemis II was among the most important developments in crewed lunar exploration in 2026.

A four-person crew traveled around the Moon aboard the Orion spacecraft and returned safely to Earth [19].

This was the first crewed journey around the Moon since Apollo 17, making it a historic milestone.

The game presents this mission as a special lunar-flyby exploration experience linked to authentic Artemis II imagery, scientific observations, and mission information.

6. THE WARNING GUIDE — LIFE IN SPACE AND ASTRONAUT HEALTH

One of CHICK TO MARS's important educational features is the Warning Guide.

Space exploration involves more than reaching another world. On long-duration missions, astronauts must protect their health, maintain proper nutrition and hydration, monitor environmental conditions, and preserve physical performance.

NASA's Human System Risks research investigates the effects of spaceflight on the human body and human performance [20–22].

Selected topics from this research are presented in simplified, age-appropriate language in the Warning Guide.

The guide covers the following key topics:

Adaptation to altered gravity: Microgravity and different gravitational conditions during spaceflight can affect the body's balance systems.

Dizziness and spatial orientation: Changes in balance and motion perception can affect mission performance.

Nutrition and hydration: Adequate food and fluid intake are vital to astronaut health.

Oxygen and environmental conditions: Life-support systems require ongoing monitoring.

Muscle and bone health: Physical activity is important during extended space missions.

Radiation: Exposure to radiation in space is a risk that must be considered when protecting human health.

Sleep and psychological adaptation: Sleep schedules, isolation, and communication within a crew can also affect mission success.

The chick's health status may change periodically during gameplay. When an alert appears, the player can open the Warning Guide and read the scientific explanation of the condition.

The player can then improve the chick's condition using game systems such as rest areas, food and water supplies, or exercise stations.

The Warning Guide is not a medical diagnostic tool. Health conditions within the game are simplified simulations used to teach scientific concepts.

7. GAME SYSTEMS AND FEATURES

7.1. Resource Management

To survive on the Moon and Mars, players must manage essential resources.

Resources include:

·   Oxygen

·   Water

·   Feed

·   Energy

·   Credits

·   Science Points

Resource production and consumption are governed by simulated in-game values.

Water and feed are produced through a shared production unit. The machine interface is divided into two separate sections:

·   Water Production

·   Feed Production

This allows the player to manage the production of the two resources independently.

Production times and consumption amounts are set for gameplay balance. They are not presented as real engineering specifications for NASA life-support systems.

7.2. Mini-Games

Mini-games can be accessed directly from the main gameplay screen.

Space Parkour: Players answer science and space questions while progressing between platforms.

Mission Quiz: Players answer questions about astronomy, space missions, and planetary science.

Rover Rescue: Players guide a rover across Mars-like terrain, collect samples, and reach a destination.

Signal Memory: Players memorize and reproduce communication-signal patterns of increasing difficulty.

The mini-games are connected to the main progression system. Completing missions rewards players with experience points, Science Points, and resources.

7.3. Level and Experience System

Players earn experience points (XP) through exploration, research, missions, and mini-games.

As players level up, they unlock additional missions, technologies, exploration areas, and costumes.

This progression system introduces scientific content in manageable stages.

7.4. Daily Rewards

Players can earn rewards by logging into the game each day.

Rewards include water, feed, Credits, Science Points, and special costumes.

The daily-reward system supports progression and encourages regular participation.

7.5. Player Profiles and Email

Players can create individual profiles.

An email address is intended to identify each player's account and potentially support cross-device save synchronization in future versions.

A secure account system requires email verification, password security, and server-side storage. The prototype keeps local save functionality separate from a future online-account infrastructure.

7.6. Main Menu

The main menu contains the following sections:

·   Colony

·   Missions

·   Mini-Games

·   Warning Guide

·   Space Archive

·   Costumes

·   Profile

This structure allows convenient access to the scientific and entertainment-focused parts of the game.

8. TECHNOLOGICAL ARCHITECTURE

CHICK TO MARS is an interactive web game developed with a mobile-first approach.

Its core technologies are:

HTML5: Game structure and content organization.

CSS3: Mobile interface, visual design, animations, and responsive screen layouts.

JavaScript: Game logic, resource management, missions, mini-games, interactions, and save functionality.

The mobile-first design is intended to work with touchscreen devices.

In later development stages, the team aims to convert the existing web-based version into a native iPhone application using Capacitor and iOS development tools.

9. INNOVATIVE ASPECTS OF THE PROJECT

The central innovation of CHICK TO MARS is the translation of real space research into an interactive game experience.

Gamification of NASA data: Authentic mission records, scientific measurements, and selected data products are linked to the player's exploration experience.

Up-to-date scientific content: Newly released data and observations from missions such as Artemis II can be added to the Space Archive.

Making historic missions playable: Missions such as Opportunity, Ingenuity, and Artemis are presented through interactive scenarios.

Astronaut health education: The Warning Guide helps players understand how living in space can affect the human body.

Colony management: Players manage water, feed, oxygen, and energy while working toward a sustainable habitat.

Combining entertainment and education: Mini-games and mission systems encourage players not only to read scientific information but also to apply it.

10. EXPECTED IMPACT AND LEARNING OUTCOMES

The target audience of CHICK TO MARS is primarily children and young people interested in space, science, and technology.

The project aims to support the following learning outcomes:

·   Recognize the environmental characteristics of the Moon and Mars.

·   Learn about major NASA space missions.

·   Understand how scientific data is collected.

·   Distinguish real scientific data from gameplay simulations.

·   Develop ideas about resource management and sustainability.

·   Understand engineering challenges encountered in space missions.

·   Learn about astronaut health and living in space.

·   Strengthen research, reasoning, and problem-solving skills.

The project's long-term objective is to encourage young people to become curious about NASA's open scientific resources and to begin exploring those resources independently.

11. SCIENTIFIC ACCURACY AND DATA-USE PRINCIPLES

CHICK TO MARS distinguishes real scientific information from fictional game elements.

The chick, the NASA employee, the revenge storyline, resource-production quantities, and some mission scenarios are entirely fictional.

NASA mission dates, the functions of scientific instruments, published observations, and data products, by contrast, are based on reliable sources.

The project does not claim to incorporate every raw dataset in NASA's archives. Instead, it aims to select relevant scientific data products and use them for educational purposes.

Content may be updated when NASA releases new data. However, this does not mean that all NASA archives are automatically or continuously streamed into the game.

This distinction is essential for maintaining the project's scientific credibility.

12. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS USED

During development, ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used as an assistive tool for brainstorming, coding support, debugging, editing text, and organizing project materials.

AI-generated scientific explanations were not treated as independent scientific sources. NASA's primary-source publications were used to verify scientific information.

Project design decisions, the game narrative, and final implementation work are carried out by the project developer.

13. CONCLUSION

CHICK TO MARS is a science-focused game project that combines the humorous journey of a little chick with authentic space exploration research.

Beginning with the chick's struggle to survive on the Moon, the player discovers both historic and recent NASA missions, examines scientific information, manages resources, completes challenges, and develops a new colony on Mars.

The project's guiding principle is:

Science can be learned not only by reading, but also through discovery and experience.

CHICK TO MARS aims to make NASA's open scientific resources more accessible and interactive for younger generations.

One Little Chick. One Giant Mission.

Dedicated to: Our science teacher and everyone who inspires scientific curiosity.

No generative AI tools were used to create the game’s artwork, characters, or visual assets.

ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used solely as a supporting tool for organizing scientific information, improving project documentation, translating content into English, and refining presentation texts.

All creative and technical development of the game was carried out by the student.
